1.pericope_label: The burden of Egypt. Behold, the Lord rideth upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt: and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence ... and I will set the Egyptians against the Egyptians
debates: What caused the civil discord: Ellicott and Wesley trace it to the overthrow of the Ethiopian power and the breaking up of Egypt into a rule of twelve, Clarke gives the same sequence at length, while Calvin refuses to let the political cause stand alone and insists that nations never rise in sedition unless God sets them against one another.
outliers: Calvin dismisses without refutation the application of the first verse to the idols said to have fallen at the coming of the infant Christ, and says the passage has been perverted to prove it.

Keil and Delitzsch read three consecutive prophecies as a trilogy, on the ruling nation, the conquered nation, and both together, and explain the attention paid to Egypt by its long entanglement with the history of the kingdom of God.
Clarke sets out the political history from the anarchy after the Assyrian defeat through the twelve princes, a single fifty-four-year reign, and the Babylonian and Persian conquests.
themes: A prophecy aimed at Judah’s confidence
God coming without a foreign army
Egypt divided against itself

3.pericope_label: And the spirit of Egypt shall fail in the midst thereof ... and the Egyptians will I give over into the hand of a cruel lord ... and the waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up
debates: Who the cruel lord is: Gill rejects the Assyrian and the Babylonian and offers the twelve tyrants or the ruler who conquered them; Wesley names the same man; Clarke reads the Babylonian and then the whole Persian succession; Ellicott declines to choose among five candidates; Calvin attends to the plural noun rather than the name.

Whether the failing waters are literal or figurative: Gill reports a reading that makes them a figure for conquest and another for the failure of sea trade, and prefers the literal; Wesley works out the mechanics of the seven mouths.
outliers: Calvin notes that the Egyptians claimed to have invented learning and would have laughed at this prophecy, thinking the sea would dry up sooner than their prudence fail.
Calvin compares Egyptian confidence in the sea and the river to the people of Venice in his own day supposing themselves impregnable behind deep ditches.
Ellicott suggests the mutterers were distinguished by some form of ventriloquism, and that panic breeds oracles in Egypt as at Athens.
themes: Wisdom taken away after courage
A bondage not easily thrown off
The river that made the land fail

6.pericope_label: And they shall turn the rivers far away; and the brooks of defence shall be emptied and dried up ... the paper reeds by the brooks ... the fishers also shall mourn, and all they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament
debates: How the sixth verse should be rendered: Ellicott reads that the river stagnates and treats the second noun as a proper name for Lower Egypt rather than brooks of defence; Clarke proposes from a cognate language that the verb means to become putrid, and notes the form is very irregular.
outliers: Calvin acknowledges that the Nile was not in fact laid dry, denies that the prophet foretold what was never accomplished, and answers that such calamities are painted in a lively manner because our stupidity needs a picture set before the eyes.

Gill corrects the account that credits the twelve tyrants with a great lake and two pyramids, since only the labyrinth was theirs and the lake, made centuries earlier, helped the river rather than hurt it.
Gill dates the manufacture of paper from the reed to the prophet’s own age, against those who assign it a much later origin.
themes: A river turned aside or left to stagnate
A prediction painted larger than the event
Trades that failed with the water

9.pericope_label: Moreover they that work in fine flax, and they that weave networks, shall be confounded ... surely the princes of Zoan are fools, the counsel of the wise counsellers of Pharaoh is become brutish
debates: What the tenth verse means: Clarke lays out three unreconciled readings without choosing, one making the first word granaries, one taking the second for nets or enclosures, and the Greek turning it into strong drink, so that the mourners are makers of barley wine; Gill prefers nets on a later Hebrew usage; Ellicott abandons the fishery and reads the pillars of the state broken and the wage-earners troubled; Calvin keeps the fish-ponds.

Whether the ninth verse is about netting or weaving: Calvin hesitates, noting that nets and fishing go together, but proposes that the word means costly openwork linen and that the prophet taunts the Egyptians for clothing themselves as if in a net.
outliers: Ellicott sketches the princes as priest-magicians boasting of wisdom and ancestry and claiming to be the only counsellors, a claim the prophet challenges by asking whether they can disclose the future as he can.
Clarke notes that the eleventh verse wants a verb, reports a conjectural transposition, and thinks the Latin translator had a copy with the verb supplied.
themes: Trades that depended on the river
A verse nobody can settle
Hereditary wisdom exposed

12.pericope_label: Where are they? where are thy wise men? ... the princes of Zoan are become fools, the princes of Noph are deceived ... the Lord hath mingled a perverse spirit in the midst thereof
debates: Which cities are meant: Ellicott and Wesley identify Noph with Memphis, Ellicott weighing two derivations of the name; Calvin admits he cannot determine them and reports an opinion naming Alexandria, whose antiquity he argues against those who make Alexander its founder.

What the last phrase of the thirteenth verse means: Ellicott reads the corner-stone of the castes, describing the superiority claimed by the priest-rulers; Calvin takes it for the chief part of a building bearing the weight; Wesley for the chief counsellors; Clarke would point the word as a plural, pillars.
outliers: Calvin distinguishes three ways of knowing the future, the revelation of the Spirit, astronomy, and comparison of past events, allows the stars only conjecture, and complains of astrologers who in his own day insinuate themselves into the confidence of princes.

Calvin denies that the prophet makes God the author of the folly, calls a dispute about predestination superfluous here since open vice is being punished, and says the giddiness is strictly mingled by the adversary to whom men are delivered.
Clarke reports two manuscripts supplying a missing verb in the twelfth verse, which he thinks genuine because the following conjunction is otherwise embarrassing.
themes: Diviners asked to prophesy
Counsellors who ruined the state
A judicial blindness poured out

15.pericope_label: Neither shall there be any work for Egypt, which the head or tail, branch or rush, may do. In that day shall Egypt be like unto women ... and the land of Judah shall be a terror unto Egypt
debates: Whether the comparison to women alludes to an Egyptian custom: Calvin knows the reading that takes it of women transacting affairs of state while men did women’s work, grants the prophet may have had it in view, and rejects the conjecture since the verse threatens a judgment rather than charging a habit.

Why Judah should terrify Egypt: Gill and Clarke explain it by the road lying open after the invasion, Calvin by the Egyptians having drawn the Jews from their confidence in God and being punished for the solicitation.
outliers: Clarke reports an opinion, on a rabbi’s authority, that head and tail mean the dragon’s head and tail and are aimed at those conversant in astronomy and astrology.
Calvin compares the relation of Egypt and Judah to the look of a woman bringing a blush to the man who seduced her, once the shame is uncovered and God appears as avenger of the marriage bond.
Keil and Delitzsch note that the fear here is only slavish, but is the beginning of a turn to something better.
themes: A nation with nothing left to do
Courage struck out of a warlike people
Fear that begins a change

18.pericope_label: In that day shall five cities in the land of Egypt speak the language of Canaan, and swear to the Lord of hosts; one shall be called, The city of destruction. In that day shall there be an altar to the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt
debates: What the five cities are: Gill reports and rejects a reading making Egypt stand for Rome and the five for the kingdoms that broke away at the Reformation; Ellicott allows a round number or the actual royal cities; Calvin and Wesley read five out of six saved and only the sixth part destroyed; Henry offers both a named city and a proportion.

Whether the name is city of destruction or city of the sun: Clarke lays out manuscripts, editions and versions on both sides, a proposed identification with Leontopolis from a cognate language, and a Greek reading giving city of righteousness, and concludes that no one can say what city was meant; Ellicott is confident of a deliberate play on words announcing the demolition of the sun-idols; Calvin says those who read sun have confused two similar letters.

Whether the altar was fulfilled in the temple Onias built: Keil and Delitzsch identify this verse as the text he appealed to; Henry and Gill both refuse the fulfilment, Henry because the pious regarded it as an affront to Jerusalem, Gill because the altar meant is Christ; Calvin calls the appeal a wicked perversion; Ellicott takes the altar for one of witness rather than rival worship.
outliers: Henry writes that converting grace, by changing the heart, changes the language, since out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.
Calvin warns against seeking harmony by a middle course, as those do who overturn religion and still wish to be thought peace-makers.
Ellicott traces four stages of Jewish influence in Egypt, from settlers on the frontier to the emigration to Alexandria and the Greek translation of the Scriptures.
themes: Comfort breaking out of the clouds
A city named for the sun or for ruin
An altar claimed and disowned

20.pericope_label: And it shall be for a sign and for a witness unto the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt ... and the Lord shall be known to Egypt ... and the Lord shall smite Egypt: he shall smite and heal it
debates: Whether the sacrifice and oblation are literal or symbolic: Ellicott poses it as a question, notes that the builders of the rival temple took the literal view, and inclines to the other; Calvin answers outright that sacrifices would be useless after the manifestation of Christ and reads confession of faith under the shadow of the ceremonies.

How the smiting is to be construed: Calvin rejects the rendering that God will strike with a wound that may be healed as weakening the sense, since the wounds themselves are the means of recovery; Ellicott answers the apparent change of tone by looking past the chastisement.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch find at least a magnificent prelude to the fulfilment in the state of Egypt before it fell to Islam in the seventh century.
Ellicott marks what he calls the catholicity of the prophet’s mind, that the highest blessing was not the exclusive inheritance of Israel but shared with a hereditary enemy.
Calvin turns the promise on his own age, wishing the world would learn the lesson after calamities enough to bring it to the brink.
themes: A saviour promised to the oppressor’s victims
Knowledge as the foundation of worship
Wounds that are the means of recovery

23.pericope_label: In that day shall there be a highway out of Egypt to Assyria ... in that day shall Israel be the third with Egypt and with Assyria ... blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel mine inheritance
debates: What the last clause of the twenty-third verse means: Calvin sets out both readings, that the two nations will serve God and that those who once burned to injure one another will now desire to do each other kindness, and expressly leaves every reader to take what he thinks best.

When the prophecy is fulfilled: Clarke and Ellicott point to the period when the three countries lived under one government, Ellicott adding that like other bright ideals it still waits for complete fulfilment; Gill and Wesley refer it chiefly to the gospel; Clarke says at the close that it remains partly to be fulfilled.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch observe that Israel’s position between the two empires had hitherto been nothing but a disadvantage, as the history of both its kingdoms proves.

Calvin distinguishes the three titles, the people of God sharing an honour once peculiar to the Jews, the work of his hands being the title proper to the Church, and Israel keeping the prerogative of the first-born.
themes: Old enemies given a road between them
A league of three with Israel the third
Titles once exclusive shared out
